phonemes.desc: Rough breathing on short alpha — the name expires outward, like a breath seen in cold air.
Delta plus long eta, the long vowel that opens the name into the unseen.

pronunciation.approximation: 'HAH-dace' — the first syllable is pitched high and sharp; the second is long and level, like the floor of the underworld.

kin.label: PIE
kin.form: *weyd-, 'to see' — the same root gives Greek οἶδα (oida), 'I know', and, with the privative ἀ-, the form ἀ-ϝιδ- (a-wid-), 'unseen'

pronunciation.note: Hádēs is Tier 1 because the Greek Ἅιδης contains both stress (acute on the first alpha) and length (long η). The name literally means 'the Unseen,' and the acute on the first syllable gives it the force of a warning.

domains.title: The Unseen King
domains.subtitle: The Dead, Wealth, and the Underworld
domains.lead: Hádēs is the necessary god — the one everyone meets and no one chooses. Not evil and not a devil, he is the impartial king of the dead, the lord beneath the earth from whose realm nothing returns unchanged. His myths concern the boundary between life and death: who may cross it, at what price, and why the boundary must hold.

cards.name: The Underworld
cards.desc: Not a place of torment but the common destination of all mortals, ruled with strict impartiality.

cards.name: Wealth of the Earth
cards.desc: As Plouton he owns gold, silver, and the fertility that rises from below — riches and graves in one vault.

cards.name: The House of Hádēs
cards.desc: A place of shadow, gates, and the three-headed Kérberos, who allows entry but not exit.

cards.name: Immovable Justice
cards.desc: Unlike other gods, Hádēs almost never intervenes in human affairs; his realm runs on procedure, not passion.

symbols.name: Cornucopia
symbols.meaning: Wealth and the fertility of the earth — his name Plouton means 'the Rich One'.

symbols.name: Bident or sceptre
symbols.meaning: The two-pronged fork of sovereignty over the dead — the underworld's answer to Poseidon's trident.

symbols.name: Kérberos
symbols.meaning: The three-headed hound at the gates — the boundary between life and death made flesh; Orpheus charmed him, Heracles dragged him up.

symbols.name: Cypress
symbols.meaning: The mourning tree, planted at graves, marking the border of his kingdom.

symbols.name: Narcissus
symbols.meaning: The flower that lured Persephonē — Zeus's trap, 'a marvel for gods and mortals alike' (Hymn to Demeter 10–12).

symbols.name: Key
symbols.meaning: He holds the keys to the underworld's gates — Aiakos, in later tradition, is their keeper.

mythology.lead: Hádēs appears rarely in Greek myth because his realm is separate from the world of the living — and the Greeks preferred it that way. His stories all concern the boundary: how Persephonē crossed it, how Orpheus almost crossed back, and why the door only opens inward.

myths.title: The Seizure of Persephonē
myths.text: The Homeric Hymn to Demeter gives the underworld its founding story. Persephonē, daughter of Demeter, was gathering flowers — roses, crocus, violets, and 'the wondrous narcissus, a trap planted by Zeus to please Hades' (5–15) — when the earth gaped and Hádēs burst up in his golden chariot 'with the consent of Zeus' and carried her down, 'weeping and crying aloud' (30–32). No one heard her — no god, no mortal; only Hekátē, from her cave, and the Sun, whose testimony later convicts the sky (24–32, 62–90). Demeter's grief stopped the seasons: seed lay hidden, famine stalked the fields, and humanity faced extinction. The settlement brokered by Zeus splits the year — two-thirds above with her mother, one-third below — 'and while she is with the strong king below, the fields are barren' (399–413, 441–470). The myth is read variously: abduction, arranged marriage, seasonal allegory. What it never forgets is that the arrangement had to be negotiated with the daughter's consent — and that the dead, like the seed, must be buried before anything grows.

myths.title: The Judges of the Dead
myths.text: What happens after the ferryman? The developed tradition — later than Homer, who knows only the dreary meadow of Asphodel — gives the dead three judges: Minos, whom Homer already sees 'holding a golden scepter, dealing judgments among the dead' (Odyssey 11.568–571); Rhadamanthys, who in the Odyssey rules in the Elysian plain (4.564); and Aiakos, keeper of the keys. Plato's Socrates (Gorgias 523e–524a) rationalizes the office with his usual irony: the judges must be naked souls judging naked souls, stripped of the wealth and fine clothes that corrupt verdicts above. The good go to the Isles of the Blessed, the curable to purification, the incurable to Tartarus. Hádēs himself is barely in these scenes — and that is the point: the underworld runs on procedure, not passion. In no other god's realm is law so absolute; the king who owns everything interferes with almost nothing.

myths.title: Orpheus and Eurydikē
myths.text: The musician Orpheus descended to bring back Eurydikē, bitten by a snake on her wedding day. Vergil (Georgics 4.453–527) gives the canonical scene: Orpheus charms Kérberos to stillness and moves the very halls of Dis, until 'the bloodless shades... wept' — and Hádēs and Persephonē grant the condition: lead her up, but do not look back. At the threshold, love and doubt collide; Orpheus turns, and 'she cried out farewell... as down she fled'. Ovid (Metamorphoses 10.1–63) adds the detail that Hades wept — the god who receives everyone unmoved was moved by song. The versions differ on who set the condition and whether Eurydikē was ever really following; the meaning holds in all of them. The law of the dead is not cruelty but the last law that cannot bend — even for the man who made the stones weep and the king of shadows shed a tear.

myths.title: The Cap of Invisibility
myths.text: Among the Cyclopes' three gifts to the sons of Krónos was a helmet for Hádēs that makes its wearer unseen — and the god, who is himself 'the Unseen', occasionally lends out his own nature. In the Iliad (5.844–845), Athēnâ 'placed on her head the cap of Hades' to confront Árēs without being seen; Apollodorus (2.4.2) sends Perseus down to fetch the same helmet for his assault on the Gorgons, along with the winged sandals and the kibisis. The object literalizes the god's theology: his power is the power of not being perceived. Greek religion kept Hádēs almost entirely out of temples and cult — no Olympian share of the cosmos, no throne on Olympus, almost no prayer addressed to him — because to see him was already to have crossed his line. His helmet lets the living borrow, briefly, the dead's defining condition: present, and unperceived.

myths.title: Theseus and Peirithoös
myths.text: The boldest attempt on the underworld was a marriage plot. Theseus and Peirithoös, having sworn to wed daughters of Zeus, descended to Hádēs' halls to claim Persephonē herself — for Peirithoös, the proudest match in the cosmos. The god received them with the hospitality of the damned: seats were offered, and the seats took hold of them; the 'chair of forgetfulness' bound them fast (Apollodorus, Epitome 1.23–24; Diodorus 4.63). Hēraklēs, come on his own mission to fetch Kérberos, tore Theseus free — leaving pieces of the chair, and by some accounts pieces of Theseus, behind; Peirithoös, who had planned the abduction, stayed forever. The story is a parody of courtship that ends as a parable: the underworld's hospitality is irreversible. Hádēs does not pursue sinners and punishes almost no one himself; he simply never lets go. The intruders' crime was not wickedness but scale — they tried to steal from the one god whose property is everything and whose door only opens inward.

lore.syncretism: The Romans called him Pluto or Dis Pater — names that emphasize his wealth rather than his dread, since speaking 'Hades' itself was ill-omened. In the mystery cults, above all the Eleusinian Mysteries, he and Persephonē — there the august couple, often called 'Theos' and 'Thea', the God and the Goddess — promised initiates a better lot after death, and ancient witnesses from Herodotus to Cicero attest the hope they offered. Christian writers later used 'Hades' both for the underworld itself and, in the New Testament, as the temporary abode of the dead — a neutral holding place, not hell. The medieval church absorbed his imagery into its devils, a darkening the Greek original never warranted. The name passed into English as the word for the realm of the dead, though the Greek god behind it is morally neutral — a king, not a torturer.
lore.culturalLegacy: Hádēs remains the archetype of the underworld ruler in Western imagination — but almost always darker than his Greek original. Unlike the Christian devil, he is neither tempter nor torturer; he is the strict, fair administrator of death, and the Greeks who named him preferred not to speak his name at all, using 'Plouton' or periphrases instead. The Eleusinian Mysteries, which honored Demeter and Persephonē with Hádēs at their center, were among the most important religious institutions of the ancient Mediterranean and shaped later ideas of salvation. Modern fantasy keeps rediscovering him: in film, games, and novels he ranges from villain to weary bureaucrat — proof of how much room the 'necessary god' leaves for reinterpretation. Restoring Hádēs restores the name of the god who receives everyone in the end.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Hádēs is the god we do not want to meet. Not because he is cruel, but because meeting him means the story is over. He is the final impartiality: rich and poor, hero and coward, all pass through his gates. The Greeks found this terrifying but also just — there is no favoritism in death, no negotiation, no appeal.

In a culture that often denies death, Hádēs is a corrective. He does not threaten; he waits. The restoration of his name in Unicode is a small acknowledgment that the Greeks had a vocabulary for the end of life that was neither sentimental nor despairing — simply true. Every temple in this lexicon is, in the long run, one of his annexes; his is the only kingdom that never loses a subject.
lore.archaeology: Eleusis preserves the Telesterion and the Ploutonion, the cave from which Hades was said to have burst to seize Persephonē — the myth's address. The Nekromanteion at Ephyra on the Acheron was an oracle of the dead, identified since antiquity with Odysseus's descent in the Nekyia. In Asia Minor, the Ploutonion at Hierapolis (Pamukkale) enclosed a fumarole of suffocating gases as the sanctuary of Pluto, lethal to birds, harmless — the priests demonstrated — to the initiated. Votive reliefs from Locri Epizephyrii and Athens show the god and goddess enthroned, Kérberos at their feet, receiving the worship of mortals who hoped for a gentler welcome.
